sections.title: Why this gets asked

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this, so this page was written for the site, as of October 2026. Tools and versions change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on details.

blocks: "The API became slow in production. What do you do?" is a favourite question for experienced candidates, because the order you do things in shows real experience. The method matters more than knowing every tool.

blocks.title: Incident flow
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Alert or user report] --> B[Assess impact: who, how many, since when]
  B --> C{Did something just change?}
  C -->|yes| D[Roll back or disable the flag first]
  C -->|no| E[Mitigate: scale, shed load, fail over]
  D --> F[Service recovered]
  E --> F
  F --> G[Find the root cause from metrics, logs, traces]
  G --> H[Fix and add a test or alert]
  H --> I[Blameless review]
blocks.caption: Restore service first. Understanding comes after users stop hurting.

rows: Traces, connection pool wait, thread dump
Pool exhausted, slow dependency, lock contention
Timeouts, pool sizing, fix the slow query
Slow query log, `EXPLAIN`, Hibernate SQL count
Fetch join or batch size, add an index
GC logs, heap dump, dominator tree
Bound it, clean up, fix the retention path
Hot loop, regex backtracking, GC thrashing
Fix the code, or size the heap
Config diff, recent changes, startup logs
Load balancer logs, keep-alive and timeouts
blocks.caption: The guides on JVM, databases, Kafka and networks explain each of these in depth.

blocks.code:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print                       # thread dump: BLOCKED threads, pool states
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info                       # heap usage now
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof        # heap dump, then open in Eclipse MAT
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000                      # GC activity every second
top -H -p <pid>                               # busiest threads of the process
kubectl logs <pod> --previous                 # logs of the crashed container
kubectl describe pod <pod>                    # OOMKilled? failed probes?
blocks.title: First-response toolkit
Gotcha
blocks.text: A heap dump pauses the JVM and may contain user data and secrets. On a busy service, take it from one instance out of rotation, and handle the file as sensitive.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: **Tell me about a production issue you handled.** A strong answer gives the impact in numbers, how it was noticed and mitigated, the root cause, the fix, and what was added so it cannot recur. As a fresher you will not have an on-call story: debug a real problem in your own project under load, and tell that story honestly.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Mitigate first, then investigate.
- Ask what changed: most incidents follow a change.
- Check traces, metrics, then logs, then dumps.
- Every incident ends with a test or an alert.

items.question: An API went from 100 ms to 3 s after a deploy. What is your first action?
items.answer: Confirm the impact and correlate with the deploy, then roll back to restore service. Investigate the cause afterwards using the diff, traces and slow queries.

items.question: Threads are mostly waiting for a database connection. What does that suggest?
items.answer: Pool exhaustion: slow queries, long transactions, or remote calls held inside a transaction. Fix the holding time first; a bigger pool only moves the pressure to the database.

items.question: A pod restarts repeatedly and shows OOMKilled, but heap metrics look fine. Why?
items.answer: The container limit counts all process memory: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and the code cache, not only heap. Check native memory and the heap's share of the limit.
